title: Internal organization of NumPy arrays
why: Chapter 1's authoritative account of the data buffer versus shape, offset, strides and byte order, and of views made by slicing and transpose without copying; it documents NumPy's model rather than a C implementation, so the chapter's C strided-view lab must supply its own offset/bounds code.

title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
why: Its data-representation and machine-level C material supplies chapters 1-3's byte addressing, unsigned/two's-complement bit operations, sign extension, locality and IEEE 754 layout and rounding from a systems-programming viewpoint; it is a general systems text and predates BF16 and tensor views, so pair it with the NumPy and Intel sources.

title: BFLOAT16 – Hardware Numerics Definition
why: Chapter 2's vendor specification for the BF16 format and FP32-to-BF16 conversion, documenting the FP32-truncated mantissa, round-to-nearest-even option, FP32 accumulation, and the explicit denormal-flush/DAZ choice that shows why BF16 subnormal handling is implementation-dependent; it is Intel's 2018 proposal, not the IEEE 754 standard.

title: Tokenizers documentation — Components
why: Chapter 5's reference for the tokenizer contract: normalization, ByteLevel pre-tokenization that maps UTF-8 bytes to visible characters, BPE as iterative most-frequent-pair merging, special-token post-processing, and ByteLevel decoding for round trips; it describes configurable library components, not one model's exact merge-rank table or vocabulary.

title: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization
why: Chapter 6's original source for the LayerNorm re-centering and re-scaling it drops and for the RMSNorm root-mean-square reduction that replaces them; it is a training-motivation paper, so the chapter's residual and gated-MLP wiring should be checked against the Transformer paper and llama2.c.

title: Attention Is All You Need
why: Chapter 7's original definition of scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, causal masking, head splitting/recombination, and chapter 6's residual-plus-layer-normalization and position-wise feed-forward block wiring; it predates GQA, RoPE and pre-norm decoders, so those must come from later sources.

title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
why: Chapter 7's primary derivation of RoPE as position-dependent two-coordinate rotations encoded by a rotation matrix, including the relative-position behavior of rotated query/key dot products and the sequence-length flexibility claim; the paper is model-oriented rather than a CPU implementation guide.

title: llama2.c
why: A small readable C decoder for chapters 6-8: run.c implements RMSNorm, RoPE, grouped-query attention via n_kv_heads and separate KV caches, a SwiGLU feed-forward path, and temperature/top-p/argmax sampling; it is a fp32-only, hard-coded Llama 2 reference aimed at tiny models, not a performance baseline or a general tokenizer.

title: Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures
why: The original roofline paper derives attainable performance from operational intensity and machine balance, which chapter 9 needs to separate an analytic bound from a measured CPU result and to contrast prefill matrix-matrix with decode matrix-vector work; its assumptions (peak bandwidth and FLOPs as ceilings, no cache effects) are the limitations the chapter must state.

title: CUDA C++ Programming Guide
why: NVIDIA's official programming-model reference documents threads, warps, thread blocks and grids, shared memory and __syncthreads barriers, global-memory coalescing, bank conflicts, occupancy, asynchronous SIMT barriers, and warp matrix (WMMA) operations, giving chapters 10 and 11 version-pinned mechanisms and an explicitly unexecuted device listing rather than assumed GPU behavior.

title: Programming Massively Parallel Processors: A Hands-on Approach
why: The Hwu, Kirk and El Hajj textbook develops SIMT execution, memory hierarchy and coalescing, tiling with shared memory, occupancy and warp-level primitives with worked matrix-multiply case studies, supplying the pedagogical derivations for chapters 10 and 11 that the CUDA reference states only as rules; the learner may need to add a personal copy.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
why: The original paper defines exact IO-aware attention, derives online softmax with running maximum and normalizer, and proves HBM-access bounds for tiled computation, so chapter 12 can present the IO argument and its assumptions separately from approximate attention and from any particular GPU kernel or successor work-partitioning.

title: flash-attention
why: The official implementation shows the mechanism behind the paper in code: csrc/flash_attn/src/flash_fwd_kernel.h calls softmax_rescale_o per key block, tracks the running max and sum, normalizes the output accumulator, and supports causal/local masks and split-K accumulation, which chapter 12 can contrast with its CPU blockwise implementation.

title: StableHLO Specification
version: docs/spec.md on main branch, accessed 2026-10-22 (spec points to tagged releases for prior versions)
why: The official specification fixes operation semantics, types, shapes and execution constraints for a portable ML op set consumed by XLA and IREE, giving chapter 21 a concrete IR contract to compare against its toy tensor IR and to separate from a compiler pass, a runtime or a generated kernel.

title: MLIR: A Compiler Infrastructure for the End of Moore's Law
why: The MLIR design paper explains multi-level dialects, progressive lowering and reusable passes, which chapter 21 uses to situate its graph-to-loop stages in a real infrastructure and to discuss dynamic-shape specialization and unsupported-operation alternatives rather than presenting one pass as the whole compiler.

title: torch/_inductor/scheduler.py
why: TorchInductor's scheduler implements production fusion legality: can_fuse_vertical matches consumer reads against producer writes and rejects remaining memory dependencies, while horizontal fusion and WhyNoFuse reasons expose shared-consumer and liveness constraints, giving chapter 22 documented decisions to weigh against separate tuned kernels and against its own buffer-planning lab.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
why: Original PagedAttention paper for chapter 14: derives KV fragmentation and duplication as the batch-size limiter, then defines fixed-size KV blocks, per-sequence block tables, reference counts and copy-on-write sharing, with measurements against contiguous-cache baselines; note it motivates the software indirection by analogy to OS paging rather than teaching MMU page tables.

title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
why: Original source for chapter 15's iteration-level (continuous) batching and selective batching: explains why request-granular static batches hold finished requests and pad work, and how per-iteration scheduling changes the achievable batch; the baseline any later chunked-prefill or admission policy should be contrasted against.

title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
why: Original RadixAttention paper for chapter 16: presents KV reuse over a radix tree of token prefixes with reference-aware eviction and cache-aware scheduling, giving the historical design and its cold/warm and branching-program workload assumptions to compare against block-hash prefix caching.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
why: Primary source for chapter 13's MHA/MQA/GQA contrast: defines grouped-query attention and the uptraining recipe from multi-head checkpoints, and quantifies the KV-cache memory and quality tradeoff that sets context limits and cache-capacity arithmetic.

title: Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM
why: Original tensor/pipeline parallelism reference for chapter 23: derives column- and row-parallel projections and the exact all-reduce placement in attention and MLP blocks, plus pipeline schedule bubbles and communication-volume arguments that carry over to inference; training-oriented, so decode-time per-token traffic must be derived separately.

title: DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving
why: Original prefill/decode disaggregation source for chapter 24: frames goodput under TTFT and per-token latency constraints, attributes interference to colocated phases, and models KV handoff, placement and parallelism choices, giving the capacity argument the chapter must reproduce rather than quote peak throughput.

title: Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase Splitting
why: Complementary phase-splitting design for chapter 24: separates prefill and decode onto different machine pools and analyzes when splitting pays off versus colocated serving, including KV transfer and utilization assumptions; use it to test the alternative to DistServe's placement story.

title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
why: Primary account of the emergent outlier features that break plain per-tensor activation quantization and of the mixed-precision decomposition (outlier channels kept in FP16) that is the alternative to SmoothQuant for chapter 18's integer-accumulator and outlier-path analysis.

title: SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models
why: Defines the mathematically equivalent per-channel scaling that migrates activation outliers into weights to enable W8A8, with the migration-strength alpha and calibration details needed for chapter 18's equivalent-rescaling lab.

title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
why: Original one-shot layer-wise method using approximate second-order information, per-column quantization with error compensation and a small damped Cholesky solve, and a group-wise INT4 instantiation for chapter 19's reconstruction-error model and sequential update lab.

title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
why: Shows that activation magnitude rather than weight magnitude identifies salient channels and replaces mixed precision with per-channel equivalent scaling and a small grid search over scales, the direct contrast to GPTQ for chapter 19 and the INT4 group-scaling discussion in chapter 17.

title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
why: Introduces exact speculative decoding with draft proposal, parallel target scoring, acceptance test and normalized residual resampling that preserves the target distribution, plus the cost analysis for chapter 20's acceptance/rollback lab.

title: Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling
why: The concurrent DeepMind formulation of modified rejection sampling for speculative decoding, giving the acceptance-probability derivation and a production-scale Chinchilla 70B measurement that anchors chapter 20's cost model.

title: llama.cpp: ggml quantization reference implementation (ggml/src/ggml-quants.c)
why: Concrete blocked low-bit layout and reference code for chapter 17: q4_0 stores one FP16 scale per 32 weights, packs two signed nibbles per byte with a -8 bias, and dequantizes with shift-and-mask plus scale, while q4_1 demonstrates an asymmetric scale/min variant.

title: vLLM: RejectionSampler implementation (vllm/v1/sample/rejection_sampler.py)
why: A maintained implementation explicitly following arXiv 2211.17192 that separates accepted, recovered (residual-distribution) and bonus tokens and supplies a separate greedy path, useful for chapter 20's exact-versus-greedy verification and KV commit details.

title: Google Benchmark User Guide
why: Methodology reference for chapter 9 and later benchmarks: warmup exclusion, minimum timing duration, repeated runs and dispersion, raw JSON output, machine/context metadata, CPU versus elapsed time, and preventing optimized-away work. Use its measurement principles with the required C/Python/Go harnesses; the C++ library is not an additional lab dependency.

title: vLLM v1 BlockPool: KV block allocation, reference counts and hash-based prefix caching (vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py)
why: Pinned implementation for chapters 14 and 16: shows the actual free-block queue, ref_cnt increments/decrements, null block, cached-block eviction and block-hash keyed caching behind the PagedAttention paper, and is the concrete hash-prefix alternative to radix-tree reuse; pair with vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py and kv_cache_utils.py in the same tag for request-level allocation and hash construction.

title: graphlib — Functionality to operate with graph-like structures
why: Primary documented implementation contract for chapter 4: directed dependencies, topological order, cycle detection, ready-node execution and completion bookkeeping. The page links CPython Lib/graphlib.py for implementation research and supplies an independent standard-library oracle for the learner's tiny computation-DAG executor; teach graph vocabulary and traces before using the API.

title: Array declaration (C reference)
why: States the C rule the chapter needs for element storage: an array is a contiguously allocated sequence of objects of one element type whose count is fixed for its lifetime.

title: sizeof operator (C reference)
why: Pins what sizeof counts (the byte size of an object representation), that character types have size 1, and that a C byte's bit width is implementation-defined, which is exactly the platform assumption the lab must assert rather than assume.

title: Fixed width integer types (since C99) (C reference)
why: Documents the exact-width typedef contract: int32_t is only defined where a signed type of exactly 32 bits with no padding is available, which is what makes sizeof(int32_t) == 4 a safe lab assertion once a byte is 8 bits.

title: Arithmetic operators, pointer arithmetic and signed overflow (C reference)
why: One page carrying the three rules the bounded view rests on: pointer addition moves in elements (not bytes), the result must stay within the array or one past it, and signed overflow is undefined behavior so an intermediate sum cannot be used as a bounds check.

title: memcpy, memcpy_s (C reference)
why: memcpy's contract of copying characters and treating both objects as unsigned char arrays, the basis for alignment-safe element access without a misaligned typed dereference.

title: Objects and alignment (C reference)
why: Object representation, effective type and the strict-aliasing exceptions (compatible types, character types), which justify reading storage bytes as characters and show why access through an unrelated type is undefined.

title: Lifetime (C reference)
why: Defines storage duration and lifetime and states that access outside an object's lifetime is undefined, grounding the requirement that the backing buffer outlive every view of it.

title: ARR30-C. Do not form or use out-of-bounds pointers or array subscripts
version: SEI CERT C Coding Standard rule page, accessed 2026-10-22
why: Enumerates the C standard undefined-behavior cases for pointer arithmetic, including UB 44, which applies specifically to using a just-past-the-end pointer as the operand of an evaluated unary *, and notes that forming the one-past index itself is well defined.

title: The N-dimensional array (ndarray)
why: Versioned reference for the buffer-plus-strided-indexing model, the byte-offset formula, and C/F contiguity.

title: numpy.ndarray.strides
why: States that strides are measured in bytes, with a concrete (20, 4) example, and warns against assigning strides by hand.

title: Copies and views
why: Defines view versus copy including shared-buffer mutation, and names the operations that produce each.

title: Indexing on ndarrays
why: Documents basic slice syntax including negative bounds and negative steps, and that basic slicing returns views.

title: numpy.reshape
why: Defines reshape's index-order ('C' means last axis fastest) and its view-when-possible, copy-otherwise contract.

title: numpy.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided
why: The documented warning that manually chosen strides can point outside the buffer and create overlapping, aliased elements.

title: NumPy shape.c: PyArray_Newshape no-copy reshape attempt
why: Primary source proving non-contiguous arrays may still reshape without a copy via _attempt_nocopy_reshape.

title: NumPy mapping.c: slice-to-view construction
why: Primary source showing exactly how a slice's start, step and length become data pointer, stride and shape.

title: numpy.ravel
why: Defines ravel's C-order flattening and its 'copy only if needed' contract, with a worked ravel of a transposed array.

title: Broadcasting (NumPy user guide)
why: The authoritative statement of trailing-axis broadcasting compatibility, missing leading axes, and the failure/ValueError case.

title: numpy.broadcast_to
why: Documents broadcast_to as a read-only, typically non-contiguous view whose elements may share one memory location.

title: numpy.add
why: States that add broadcasts unequal operand shapes to a common output shape and returns a freshly allocated array unless out is supplied.

title: torch.Tensor.expand
why: Explicitly documents the zero-stride representation of an expanded size-one dimension, used here only as a cross-library demonstration of the mechanism.

title: Google Benchmark - Reducing Variance in Benchmarks
why: The measurement-methodology companion to S32: it enumerates concrete variance sources (CPU migration, turbo, SMT, context switches, other CPUs' cache effects, NUMA) and six mitigations, and it warns that shrinking a working set to fit L1 may optimize for an unrealistic situation.

title: LLVM Benchmarking tips
why: Compiler-project guidance that low noise is necessary but not sufficient because measurement bias remains, plus the practical checklist (high-resolution timer, repeated runs, disabled frequency scaling/ASLR) that justifies recording machine and compiler context.

title: clock_gettime(2) - Linux manual page
version: Linux man-pages page from man7.org, accessed 2026-10-22
why: The authoritative Linux contract for CLOCK_MONOTONIC, including that it is nonsettable, unaffected by discontinuous clock jumps but affected by frequency adjustments, and that consecutive reads may return identical values - the caveats a C elapsed-interval timer must state.

title: time - Time access and conversions
version: Python 3 documentation at docs.python.org/3, accessed 2026-10-22 (includes the 3.13 change to perf_counter)
why: Documents time.perf_counter as the highest-resolution short-duration clock, including sleep, and CPython's note that it shares time.monotonic's clock and cannot go backwards, giving the Python half of the timing contract.

title: Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong!
version: ASPLOS '09, March 7-11 2009, Washington DC; PDF course copy
why: Shows that environment size and link order change whether -O3 looks faster at all, on two microprocessors and two compilers, which is the evidence for treating one timed ordering as setup-specific rather than universal.

title: CS3130: Caches - Locality
why: A short university reading that defines spatial and temporal locality at the access-pattern level, which is all section 6 needs before introducing a traversal measurement; its cache-line and set-associativity material is deliberately left for chapter 9.

title: ISO/IEC 9899:2024 (en) — N3220 working draft
version: N3220 working draft of ISO/IEC 9899:2024 (C23), January 2024
why: Normative C text for chapter 1's storage model: array contiguity, sizeof units, exact-width int32_t, subscript and pointer rules, one-past formation versus dereference, lifetime, effective type and signed-overflow undefined behavior.

title: INT32-C. Ensure that operations on signed integers do not result in overflow
version: SEI CERT C Coding Standard rule page, accessed 2026-10-22
why: Shows that because signed overflow is undefined, implementations may trap or compile under the assumption that it never happens, which is why a bounds test placed after an overflowing offset expression is not a safety check.

title: NumPy glossary
why: Short official definitions that separate an axis (a named dimension) from its extent and from element byte size.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook: Measures of Location
why: Primary statistical definitions and explanation of median resistance to extreme tail values.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook: Measures of Scale
why: Primary definition of median absolute deviation and explanation of its reduced sensitivity to extreme observations.

title: User-Requested Performance Counters
why: Documents optional PMU-backed hardware performance counters and their libpfm/platform requirements, which chapter 1 needs alongside benchmark-supplied user counters to distinguish counted logical bytes from independently measured hardware events.

title: Built-in Types — Common Sequence Operations
why: Primary definition of stepped slices and their exclusive stop for either step sign.

title: torch.nn.Linear
why: Primary example of a model layer applying an additive bias vector to input samples.
